questions.stem: In a ministry or public agency, what is meant by 'a delegation' to an officer?
options: A group of officers sent to an overseas meeting
An informal favour agreed between colleagues
A formal grant of power to act for the holder
A request to Cabinet for extra budget

questions.stem: An officer at a ministry has been told she may now approve leave for her unit. Where should she confirm exactly what this power covers?
options: In the written instrument of delegation
In what her predecessor used to do
In a colleague's advice in the corridor
In the unit's old staff meeting notes

questions.stem: Why do public bodies delegate powers to officers below the head of the organisation?
options: So senior officers carry no further accountability
So decisions are made at the right level, promptly
So the usual laws and rules no longer apply
So each officer may set her own rules

questions.stem: A Permanent Secretary delegates a power to a director. Who remains accountable overall for how the power is used?

No one, once it has been delegated

She may approve any overtime she sees fit

questions.stem: A delegate refuses every hardship application from people over 60 because of an unwritten 'rule' in her unit, without looking at the facts. What is the main problem?

options: No, never, once it has been delegated

questions.stem: An applicant disagrees with a delegate's refusal of his permit. What should the delegate tell him?

questions.stem: Which statement about policy guidelines for delegates is correct?
options: Follow them, but still weigh each case's facts

questions.stem: Which practice best helps a director check how her delegates are using their powers?
options: Asking them once a year if all is well

questions.stem: What is the main difference between a formal delegation and simply assigning a task to an officer?
options: A task is always more important than a power

questions.stem: An officer approves a grant with a one-word email, 'Approved', with no reference to her authority. What is the main risk?
options: The grant will be paid twice

questions.stem: While her decision on his application is pending, an applicant offers a delegate a gift basket. What should she do?

options: Accept it, as the other 13 were in order

questions.stem: Why should delegates decide matters within the organisation's service standards?
options: Late decisions are always invalid

questions.stem: Which conduct best shows integrity in using a delegated power?

questions.stem: Why should a delegation be given in writing rather than by word of mouth?

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

essays.stem: Explain what a delegation is in a public body, why delegations are used, and the responsibilities of an officer who receives one.
essays.modelAnswer: A delegation is a formal, usually written, grant of power from a person or body that holds it, such as a minister, permanent secretary, board or chief executive, to another officer, so that the officer can make decisions or take actions in their place. It is different from simply being given a task, because it carries the legal authority to decide. Delegations are used so that the large number of routine decisions in a public body can be made promptly at the right level, by officers who know the matters well, while senior leaders concentrate on policy and strategy. An officer who receives a delegation must first understand it: what powers it covers, the financial or other limits, the conditions and whether it may be passed on. She must act only within it and refer anything outside it. She must make decisions lawfully, fairly and for the proper purpose, on relevant evidence, and declare any conflict of interest. She must record her decisions and reasons, report as required, and remember that she is answerable for her decisions while the delegator remains accountable overall.
markingPoints: Defines a delegation as a formal grant of power, not just a task
Explains why delegations are used
Delegate must know the scope, limits and conditions
Acts lawfully, fairly and within limits, declaring conflicts
Records, reports and is accountable

essays.stem: Describe the steps a delegate should follow when making a decision under a delegated power, from receiving the matter to recording the outcome.
essays.modelAnswer: When the matter arrives, the delegate first checks that it falls within her delegation: the type of decision, any financial limit and any conditions. If it does not, or she is unsure, she refers it or seeks advice. She checks whether she has any conflict of interest and, if so, declares it and steps aside. Next she identifies the law, policy and guidelines that apply and what matters she must consider. She gathers the relevant evidence and, where her decision may harm someone, tells that person the concerns and gives them a fair chance to respond. She then weighs the evidence against the criteria, considering the facts of this case rather than applying a blanket rule, and ignoring irrelevant matters such as personal views or outside pressure. She makes the decision within the service time. She records the decision, the delegation she used, the evidence and the reasons, and files it. Finally, she tells the person the outcome, with reasons and any right of review, and includes the decision in her regular report to the delegator.
markingPoints: Confirms the matter is within the delegation, or refers it
Checks for conflicts of interest
Identifies applicable law and policy and gathers evidence
Gives procedural fairness and weighs the case on its merits
Records, informs with reasons and review rights, and reports

essays.stem: Explain five principles of good decision-making that apply when an officer exercises a delegation, giving a public-sector example of each.
essays.modelAnswer: First, act within power: an officer whose delegation covers trade licences must not decide building permits. Second, consider only relevant matters: when deciding a hardship grant, the officer should look at the applicant's income and needs as the policy requires, not at whether the applicant has complained before. Third, give procedural fairness: before cancelling a vendor's licence for breaches, the officer should tell the vendor the concerns and listen to his reply, and should not decide if she is biased, for example because the vendor is a relative. Fourth, use the power for its proper purpose: a power to transfer staff for operational needs must not be used to punish a colleague. Fifth, exercise real judgement: the officer should apply guidelines but still consider each case, rather than refusing all applications from a group under an unwritten rule, and she should decide herself rather than simply following a politician's instruction. In addition, decisions should rest on evidence and be recorded with reasons, so that they can be explained and reviewed.
markingPoints: Acting within power, with an example
Relevant and irrelevant considerations, with an example
Procedural fairness and freedom from bias, with an example
Proper purpose, with an example
Genuine judgement, not rigid rules or dictation, with an example

essays.stem: A director's delegation allows her to approve spending of up to J$1,500,000 a transaction and J$6,000,000 in total a quarter, if budget is available and the procurement rules are followed. She has already approved J$4,500,000 this quarter. Three requests arrive: A for J$1,200,000, B for J$1,800,000, and C for J$900,000 from a supplier owned by her cousin. Decide what she should do with each, and justify your answers.
essays.modelAnswer: Request A is for J$1,200,000, which is within the transaction limit of J$1,500,000. Adding it to the J$4,500,000 already approved gives J$5,700,000, which is within the quarterly limit of J$6,000,000. She may approve A, provided she confirms that budget is available and the purchase followed the procurement rules. After approving it she would have only J$300,000 left for the quarter. Request B, at J$1,800,000, is above her transaction limit, so she must not approve it, and must not split it into smaller orders. She should refer it to the officer whose delegation covers that amount, with her recommendation. Request C raises two problems. The supplier is owned by her cousin, so she has a conflict of interest; she must declare it and take no part in the decision. Also, after approving A, she could approve only J$300,000 more this quarter, so C would exceed her quarterly limit anyway. C should therefore be referred to another authorised officer, with the conflict recorded. She should record each decision and referral, with reasons, in her monthly delegation report.
markingPoints: A: J$5,700,000 total is within both limits; approve if conditions are met
B: exceeds the transaction limit; refer, do not split
C: conflict of interest must be declared and she steps aside
C would also exceed the remaining J$300,000
Records and reports each decision

essays.stem: Describe how a delegate in a public body should identify and manage conflicts of interest when making decisions.
essays.modelAnswer: A conflict of interest arises when an officer's private interests, or those of family, friends or business associates, could improperly influence, or be seen to influence, an official decision. The delegate should check for conflicts at the start of every matter, by looking at who the applicants, bidders or suppliers are and asking whether she has any personal, family, financial or social link with them. She should also consider gifts or hospitality offered, past disputes and outside work. A perceived conflict matters as much as a real one, because public trust depends on decisions being seen as fair. If a conflict exists, she should declare it in writing to her manager or the delegator, as the organisation's policy requires, and record it in the conflicts register. Usually she should step aside from the decision so that another authorised officer handles it, and she should not try to influence that officer. Where the conflict is minor, the manager may agree other safeguards, such as a second reviewer. She should decline gifts from people whose matters she is deciding and keep her declarations up to date.
markingPoints: Defines real and perceived conflicts
Checks for conflicts at the start of each matter
Declares in writing and records in the register
Steps aside or follows agreed safeguards
Declines gifts and keeps declarations up to date

essays.stem: Evaluate the risks of sub-delegation and acting arrangements in a government agency, and recommend controls to manage them.
essays.modelAnswer: Sub-delegation and acting arrangements keep work moving when the main delegate is absent or overloaded, so that the public does not wait for decisions. However, they carry risks. Sub-delegation may not be allowed by the instrument or the law, so decisions made under it could be invalid. Powers may pass to officers without the knowledge, training or seniority to use them well. It may become unclear who holds which power, and the delegator may lose track of how it is used. Acting officers may use powers when the acting appointment has not been made formally, or continue to use them after the post-holder returns. To manage these risks, the agency should state clearly in each instrument whether sub-delegation is allowed and on what conditions. Acting appointments should be made in writing, with start and end dates, and recorded in the delegations register. Instruments should be made to positions, including acting holders, where the law allows. Officers receiving powers should be briefed or trained. All decisions should record the delegation used, and regular reports and sample reviews should show whether powers are being used correctly.
markingPoints: Recognises the benefit of continuity
Risks: invalid decisions, unprepared officers, loss of oversight
Risks of informal or open-ended acting arrangements
Controls: clear instruments, written acting appointments, register
Controls: training, recorded authority and monitoring

essays.stem: Describe how the head of a public agency should set up and maintain a sound framework of delegations.
essays.modelAnswer: The head should start by identifying the powers the agency holds under its laws, regulations and government policies, including financial, procurement, human resource and operational powers, and checking which of them may lawfully be delegated. She should decide, for each power, the right level at which decisions should be made, balancing speed and local knowledge against risk. Each delegation should be set out in a written instrument, made to positions rather than named people, stating the power, the limits, any conditions, whether sub-delegation is allowed and any reporting duty. All delegations should be recorded in a single register that is easy for staff and auditors to consult. Officers should be told of their delegations and trained in using them and in good decision-making. The framework should include reporting, such as monthly reports of financial approvals, and regular sample reviews by managers or internal audit. The head should review the framework at least once a year, and whenever laws, structures or risks change, varying or revoking delegations that are no longer suitable and updating the register.
markingPoints: Identifies the agency's powers and which can be delegated
Sets the right level for each decision
Written instruments to positions with limits and conditions
Register, communication and training
Reporting, monitoring and regular review

essays.stem: A delegate at a parish municipal corporation is considering cancelling a food vendor's licence after reports of unsafe practices. Explain how procedural fairness applies and the steps she should take.
essays.modelAnswer: Procedural fairness means that a person whose rights or interests may be harmed by a decision is told the case against them, has a fair chance to respond, and has the matter decided by someone without bias. Cancelling a licence would take away the vendor's living, so these duties clearly apply. The delegate should first check that cancellation is within her delegation and that she has no conflict of interest with the vendor. She should gather the evidence, such as inspection reports, photographs and complaints, and check that it is reliable. She should then write to the vendor setting out the specific concerns, the evidence relied on and the possible outcome, and give a reasonable time to respond in writing or at a meeting. She should consider the response with an open mind, together with any steps the vendor has taken to put things right, and whether a lesser action, such as a warning or conditions, would be enough. She should then decide, record her reasons, and tell the vendor the decision, the reasons and how to seek a review.
markingPoints: Explains the hearing and no-bias elements
Confirms authority and no conflict
Gathers reliable evidence and tells the vendor the case in writing
Gives a fair chance to respond and considers it with an open mind, including lesser options
Decides with recorded reasons and explains review rights

essays.stem: An officer discovers that two weeks ago she approved a payment that was above her delegated limit. Describe what she should do, and explain why.
essays.modelAnswer: She should act at once and openly, because a decision outside a delegation may be invalid and public money may have been spent without proper authority. First, she should check the facts: the amount, her limit, the date and whether the payment has already been made. She should then report the matter promptly to her manager and the delegator, in writing, explaining what happened and why. Hiding it, or trying to correct it quietly, would make the breach more serious and damage trust. The officer who holds the right level of delegation would need to consider the payment and decide whether to confirm it, if that is allowed, or take steps to deal with it, following the finance rules and advice. She should cooperate with any review. She should then work out why the error happened, for example because she misread the limit, the system did not block it, or the payment was split. She should suggest improvements, such as a system check on limits or clearer guidance, and make sure her own future approvals stay within her delegation.
markingPoints: Recognises the decision may be invalid and acts at once
Checks the facts
Reports openly in writing to the manager and delegator
Leaves the remedy to the officer with proper authority
Finds the cause and suggests improvements

essays.stem: Justify why decisions made under delegation must be recorded with reasons, and describe what a good decision record contains.
essays.modelAnswer: Recording decisions with reasons is essential to accountability in the public service. It shows that the officer had the authority to decide and used it properly. It lets the person affected understand the decision, accept it or seek a review on an informed basis. It allows managers, internal auditors and review bodies to check that the power was used lawfully, fairly and consistently. It protects the officer, because a clear record shows that she acted in good faith on the evidence, even if the decision is later questioned. It also helps future officers to make consistent decisions in similar cases. A good decision record states the matter and the applicant, the date, the officer's name and position, and the delegation or power used. It lists the evidence considered and any submissions from the person affected. It sets out the criteria from the law or policy, the findings on the key facts and how the criteria were applied to reach the decision. It notes any conflict declared and how it was managed, the decision itself, any conditions, and how the person was told, including their review rights.
markingPoints: Shows authority was held and used properly
Allows the person to understand the decision and seek review
Allows oversight and protects the officer
Supports consistency
Lists the contents of a good record

practical1.title: Decide applications under a delegation and record the decisions
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a case pack for a made-up public body (for example a parish municipal corporation licensing unit, or a ministry's small grants programme). It contains an instrument of delegation with limits and conditions, the relevant policy and criteria, and six application files, some of which fall outside the delegation, involve a conflict of interest or need the applicant to be heard first. As a group, each member takes at least one file and the group produces: a decision record for each file (the power used, evidence, criteria, findings, decision and reasons), or a referral note where the file is outside the delegation or a conflict exists; a letter to each applicant giving the outcome, the reasons and the right of review; a register listing all six decisions; and a one-page monthly report to the delegator. Give each member a named role: lead delegate (checks every file against the instrument first and writes the report), two decision-makers, a fairness and conflicts officer (checks that each person was heard and conflicts declared), and a records officer (keeps the register and checks the letters). In a group of four, the lead delegate also keeps the register. Photograph or screenshot each stage.
materials: Case pack from the assessor: instrument of delegation, policy and six application files
Computers with word-processing and spreadsheet software, and a printer
photos: The flipchart showing each file checked against the delegation
A referral note for a file outside the delegation or with a conflict
The monthly report to the delegator
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Checked each file against the limits and conditions before deciding
Referred files outside the delegation and handled the conflict correctly
Based decisions on the criteria and evidence, with clear reasons
Gave the applicant a fair hearing where the decision could harm them
Letters are clear, polite and state the right of review
safety: Use only the made-up case files and invented names
Keep personal information in the files confidential to the group and the assessor
Discuss cases respectfully and without judging the applicants as people
Share the workload fairly and take short screen breaks

practical2.title: Review a delegations register and brief managers on a revised instrument
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a case pack for a made-up government agency that has just restructured: an old delegations register, the new organisation chart, a list of the agency's powers, and recent audit comments (for example, delegations held by named people who have left, missing limits, and unclear acting arrangements). As a group, produce: a gap analysis in a spreadsheet comparing each current delegation with the new structure and noting problems; a revised instrument of delegation for one division, made to positions, with limits, conditions, rules on sub-delegation and acting, and reporting duties; an updated register for that division; and a ten-minute briefing, with no more than six slides, for the division's managers. Deliver the briefing to the assessor and another group acting as managers, and answer their questions. Give each member a named role: project lead (keeps time and chairs the briefing), register analyst (builds the gap analysis), instrument drafter, register keeper (updates the register), and briefing designer (prepares the slides; every member presents a part). In a group of four, the project lead also updates the register. Photograph or screenshot each stage.
materials: Case pack from the assessor: old register, new organisation chart, list of powers and audit comments
Computers with spreadsheet, word-processing and presentation software
photos: The gap analysis spreadsheet on screen
The updated register for the division
The group delivering the briefing, showing each presenter
The list of managers' questions and the answers given
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Found the main gaps and problems in the old register
Revised instrument is made to positions with clear limits and conditions
Sub-delegation, acting and reporting rules are clear
Briefing explains managers' duties accurately in plain language
Answered questions correctly or noted them for follow-up
Worked respectfully and shared the work fairly
safety: Use only the made-up case and invented names
Keep the case pack confidential to the group and the assessor
Speak respectfully and let every member contribute
Keep cables tidy and the presentation area clear
